summary: Reviews the security threats to marking signalling messages as emergency calls and to mapping a caller's location to the URI of the right Public Safety Answering Point. From these threats it derives security requirements for such systems. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Internet emergency calls need to reach the right public safety answering point. This RFC describes attacks on call marking and location mapping, then lists security requirements to reduce those risks.

questions: how are emergency calls routed to a psap securely
what security requirements apply to emergency call mapping
subtitle: Threats to marking emergency calls and mapping caller locations to public safety answering points.

tldr.problem: IP emergency calls use an emergency identifier and a mapping service that turns a caller's location into a Public Safety Answering Point address. Attackers may misuse either part to misroute calls or expose information.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes attacker goals and attacks, then sets requirements for call routing and the mapping protocol, including integrity, response authentication, confidentiality, and resistance to flooding.
tldr.outcome: It provides security requirements for designers of emergency marking and mapping systems. It is an Informational RFC.

today: RFC 5069 is an Informational RFC published in January 2008, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sets security requirements for emergency marking and mapping without specifying a mapping protocol.

sections.title: Emergency Marking and Mapping
sections.content:
IP-based emergency calling uses an emergency service identifier to mark call signaling and a mapping protocol to translate the identifier and caller location into a URI for a Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP). A mapping client sends location information to a mapping server and receives a URI that can direct the call to a PSAP.

The RFC covers attacks on emergency marking and location-to-PSAP mapping. Verifying whether an incident is genuine and other attacks involving false location information are outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: An emergency call needs a marker that identifies it as an emergency and a mapping result that points to a PSAP. This RFC focuses on attacks against those two steps.

sections.title: What Attackers May Try to Do
sections.content:
An attack may target the emergency response system or one person. System-level goals include denying service in an area, using the emergency identifier to bypass normal authorization, or diverting calls to a non-emergency destination.

Attacks against an individual may prevent that person from receiving help or reveal information about the emergency. Intercepted mapping requests and replies can expose location, a PSAP URI, the emergency service identifier, and the addresses of the mapping client and server.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker may block emergency service, misuse the emergency marker to get unauthorized service, divert a call, or learn information about a caller. The RFC considers both attacks on a whole system and attacks on one person.

sections.title: Attacks on Marking and Mapping
sections.content:
A caller can misuse an emergency identifier if a provider accepts the call without normal authorization and routes it to the address supplied by the caller without checking that the destination is a PSAP. An attacker may also flood mapping clients or servers, take control of an intermediary, modify or replay mapping messages, impersonate a mapping server, or corrupt its database.

Attacks can also target a particular mapping client to prevent one person receiving aid. Intercepting mapping traffic can reveal the caller's location and the emergency service identifier, which may indicate whether the call concerns fire, police, or ambulance services.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers can misuse the emergency marker, interfere with mapping messages, impersonate a mapping server, or alter mapping data. Intercepted requests can also expose a caller's location and the type of emergency service sought.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
The call-routing entity MUST verify that the destination address is a PSAP for the calls described in the RFC. The mapping protocol MUST NOT create new flooding or amplification opportunities. A client MUST be able to check that a response matches its query, and requests and responses MUST have integrity protection.

The client MUST be able to authenticate the source of a response. Security discussions for mapping-server discovery MUST address impersonation, and the mapping protocol's security considerations MUST address database corruption. Responses SHOULD include information that can be matched with server logs. The protocol and its system MUST maintain confidentiality of requests and responses.

The RFC identifies no new protocol requirement for probing emergency call routing entities or for attacks aimed at one specific person beyond ordinary operational defenses.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules require checking that a call goes to a PSAP, that a reply answers the right request, and that messages cannot be changed or read by outsiders. The mapping protocol must also avoid enabling floods and address server impersonation and database corruption.
